scope: Verification of seven proposed 1750-1900 Buffalo and Western New York historical-place investigations, with two additional leads found in the reviewed records.
publicationStatus: Publication prepared: /research/early-industry covers the seven subjects and two further leads; /sites/williamsville-water-mills adds the surviving mill address as an explicitly qualified marker; /sites/katherine-street-peninsula gains the Farmer's Point ironmaking chapter. Other historical footprints remain unmapped. This status records the editorial disposition, not proof of successful deployment.
method: Compared candidates with existing Atlas source modules; searched institutional, government and archival sources; downloaded and extracted relevant reports; visually checked cited PDF pages. Historical accounts in agency files are historical evidence, not new environmental measurements. A catalog description verifies an archival holding, not the contents of unexamined ledger pages.

candidates.decision: Strongest new historical environmental story; prepare an attributed narrative, hold precise map pin pending footprint verification.

verified.finding: DEC recounts oil leaking from early tanks into Little Genesee Creek, recovery behind a dam, shipments to an unnamed Buffalo oil works, and a reported stock of 10,000 barrels of salvaged crude when Cynthia was built in 1882.

Local history places the works on the Porter Cowles flats at Bolivar's north end, south of Salt Rising Road on a Bradford, Eldred & Cuba Railroad siding; reports initial operation September 30, 1882 and B. W. Baum & Son ownership.

limits: Do not identify the Buffalo receiver as Sinclair or another refinery without a named shipping record.
The refinery recovered oil already in the creek; the reviewed passage does not make Cynthia the source of every upstream leak.
Historical release evidence does not establish current soil or water concentrations, exposure, site classification or cleanup status.
nextRecords: Herrick, Empire Oil (1949), relevant original pages and citations
1880s Bolivar maps, deeds, railroad siding plans, assessment rolls and petroleum trade press
Dam location and named Buffalo consignee in shipping or company records

candidates.decision: Ready for an industrial-landscape history with facility locations distinguished; no contamination designation from the reviewed sources.

verified.finding: The permanent gristmill and nearby sawmill date to 1811; the survey also records Williams's tannery, distillery, dams and raceways. The surviving landmark is at 56 Spring Street.

limits: The tannery and distillery need separate footprint evidence; do not assign all early uses to the surviving mill parcel.
Island Park raceway dates conflict: indexed LWRP text says 1814; the survey inventory uses circa 1841. Historical system existence is stronger than the exact construction date.
No site-specific contaminant analyses were established by these historical sources.
nextRecords: Earliest mill deeds and water-power rights
Nineteenth-century Williamsville maps showing tannery, distillery, dams and races
Original material underlying the survey's Howe citation and the two raceway dates

candidates.decision: Develop separate historical records for the early businesses and later Perry Street plant; North Evans has a specific archival collection lead.
candidates.period: 1840s through 1900, with a separately dated 1904 canal-condition follow-up

verified.finding: The business history distinguishes an 1844 leather store and tannery acquisition outside Buffalo, a Buffalo sheepskin tannery two years later, a North Evans enterprise, and the 1877 acquisition of Lymburner & Torrey.
The university catalog identifies original 1856-1857 hides records for North Evans and Schoellkopf-related notes; only the description, not the ledger contents, was reviewed.

The later tannery stood north of Perry between Mississippi and Liberty, beside the Clark and Skinner Canal. A cited 1904 newspaper describes refuse-contaminated canal water there without assigning all refuse to the tannery.

limits: Do not turn the 1846 Buffalo start into the founding date of the later Perry Street plant.
White's Corners/Hamburg and North Evans need parcel-level identity work.
Tannery use does not by itself establish chromium use, measured contamination, or a particular discharge route.
nextRecords: University of Waterloo SCA204-GA528-1-11 original ledger pages
Contemporary directories and atlases for the 1846 and 1877 Buffalo businesses
Original September 29, 1904 Express account and canal records
Hamburg and Evans deeds and factory water rights

candidates.decision: Ready for a district-level industrial history; separate plants and quarries before creating individual map records.

verified.finding: USGS records Jonathan Delano's 1839 Falkirk works near Akron, followed by Montgomery and Newman interests; H. Cummings & Son began another plant in 1854, followed by a later plant west of Akron.
The 1884 account distinguishes Newman, Akron Cement Works, and Cummings' Akron Cement Works; describes kilns, water and steam power, and quarry tunneling.

limits: 1824 in the USGS history refers to Williamsville, not the start of Akron production.
The 1869 versus 1871 transfer dates remain unresolved.
Historic natural cement should not automatically be described as a modern Portland-cement process; no reviewed source establishes a hazardous-waste site.
nextRecords: 1880 Beers map of Akron and historic quarry deeds
Company incorporation and sale records around 1869-1871
Separate mill, kiln, tunnel and quarry footprints along Murder Creek and west of Akron

candidates.decision: Expand the existing Katherine Street historical account first; add a separate place only if the furnace footprint and distinct story justify it.

verified.finding: Two partnerships began constructing blast furnaces at Farmer's Point, where Hamburg and Katherine streets meet the Buffalo River, in 1860-1861; the operations merged as Union Iron Works.
The regional iron-history chapter separately records the Union Iron Company in 1861 and its industrial equipment.

limits: Do not merge Farmer's Point, Hanna Furnace/Union Ship Canal and Black Rock furnace locations merely because company names overlap.
The reviewed historical accounts do not identify an off-site slag destination or establish radiological material.
Existing Katherine Street restoration and sediment findings must not automatically be attributed to the nineteenth-century furnaces.
nextRecords: 1860s-1890s fire insurance and city atlas plates
Original furnace/company directories and deeds
Crosswalk original shoreline and furnace locations to the current Katherine Street record

candidates.decision: Retain as a verified historical-place lead with an explicit founding-date conflict; use late 1820s until resolved.

verified.finding: Both historical reports place an early foundry and machine shop at Ohio and Indiana streets; the 2013 survey gives 1828 and the 2002 report gives 1826.

An 1832 directory transcription lists J. Mayhew & Co. selling pig iron, castings and related goods from a Buffalo Creek warehouse; this supports early iron-trade activity but is not proof of the foundry's full identity.

limits: Do not repeat a definitive first-foundry claim or exact founding year before reconciling sources.
Historic intersection geography is not a modern parcel boundary.
DEC archive 915029 is the Hanna record containing the regional history, not a cleanup designation for this foundry.
nextRecords: Original 1820s newspapers and directories
1850 Emslie and Kirk map cited by the 2013 survey
Earliest partnership deeds and advertisements

candidates.decision: Strong 1750s historical-landscape subject; distinguish the French and British positions and include Seneca control and portage labor.
candidates.period: 1751 onward, with a separately dated 1760 British fort

verified.finding: The state museum dates the French upper-portage post to 1751 and Fort Schlosser to 1760, describing the latter as 40 rods upstream rather than the identical footprint.
National Register documentation discusses the 1751 trading post, military stores and traffic, Seneca permission, and displacement of Seneca portage labor by horses.

limits: The earlier 1745 storehouse is context, outside the requested 1750 start.
No reviewed source establishes current contamination, a modern cleanup boundary, or a direct link to later industrial wastes.
Do not infer archaeological coordinates from redacted material or describe every property mentioned in the nomination bundle as individually listed.
nextRecords: Published period portage maps and fort plans
Severance and Pouchot source passages cited in the National Register account
Public interpretation with Seneca-authored historical context

additionalLeads.name: Warren Granger natural-cement works, Scajaquada Creek / later Forest Lawn area
additionalLeads.finding: USGS page 22 locates an 1850 natural-cement plant beside Scajaquada Creek below the Main Street bridge, in what the 1913 account calls Forest Lawn Cemetery.
additionalLeads.nextRecord: Check early cemetery acquisitions, quarry and creek maps, and directories; exact footprint and environmental findings remain unverified.

additionalLeads.name: Seneca Oil Spring and Niagara trade
additionalLeads.finding: DEC's chapter records Seneca oil use and trade at Fort Niagara by 1767, citing Herrick. This offers an Indigenous resource-history subject within the requested period.
additionalLeads.nextRecord: Consult Seneca Nation historical sources and the original historical references before a new narrative. A natural seep is not an industrial-contamination finding.
